concept.name: Trading journal
concept.definition: A systematic record of trades and the reasoning behind them - entries, exits, size, thesis, emotional state, and lessons - used to create an objective feedback loop for performance. Research on hindsight bias specifically recommends contemporaneous decision diaries because memory of past reasoning is unreliable.
concept.intuition: Your memory says you are a disciplined genius; the journal shows the trades you actually took.
concept.mechanics: Trades are logged at or near decision time with rationale and context, then analyzed for statistics (win rate, expectancy, R-distribution by setup) and behavioral patterns (rule breaks, tilt episodes). Written contemporaneous records are the principal defense against 'knew-it-all-along' memory distortion.
concept.failure_modes: Journals fail when entries are written after outcomes are known (hindsight contamination), when only narrative and no structured data is kept, or when data is collected but never analyzed. Inconsistent logging produces a database that cannot support conclusions.
concept.misconceptions: A journal is neither a diary of feelings alone nor a bare trade blotter; it is the combination of decision records plus outcomes that enables calibration. Keeping one does not automatically improve trading - only analyzed journals do.
concept.example: Three months of journaled trades reveal that a trader's average winner is 2.1R but his average loser is 1.4R because he overrides stops - a fact invisible in his memory.

citations.source: Brett N. Steenbarger, The Psychology of Trading: Tools and Techniques for Minding the Markets (Wiley, 2003) - publisher page
